title: J.P. Morgan Chase v. City of Corsicana
description: Whether economic-development grants authorized by section 52-a of the Texas Constitution are exempt from the traditional Gift Clause requirements, or if they remain subject to scrutiny regarding public purpose, controls, and non-gratuitous expenditure.
plaintiff_argument: JPMorgan Chase argued that section 52-a's "notwithstanding" clause exempts economic development grants from the pre-existing Gift Clause requirements.
defendant_argument: The City of Corsicana and Navarro County argued that section 52-a only establishes economic development as a public purpose within the traditional Gift Clause framework, meaning the grants are still subject to Gift Clause requirements, and that the closure of Gander Mountain extinguished the public purpose, making continued payments unconstitutional.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the lower courts' summary judgment, holding that economic-development grants under section 52-a are subject to Gift Clause requirements but that the closure of a specific business does not automatically extinguish the public purpose if broader economic development continues, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Muth v. Voe; Doe v. Abbott; Muth v. PFLAG
description: Whether the injunctions preventing the state from classifying gender-transition therapy for children as child abuse should be dissolved.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners (state officials) argued that the injunctions preventing the state from classifying gender-transition therapy for children as child abuse should be dissolved because the underlying legal theories are foreclosed by new laws.
defendant_argument: The respondents (families, PFLAG, Dr. Mooney) argued that the injunctions should remain, challenging the state's policy as unlawful and asserting their standing.
decision_outcome: The court dissolved the injunctions in their entirety, allowing the state's policy to classify gender-transition therapy for children as child abuse to proceed.

title: PFLAG v. Office of the Attorney General
description: Whether the Attorney General's office has a reasonable basis to demand documents from PFLAG, Inc. via a Civil Investigative Demand (CID) to investigate potential Deceptive Trade Practices Act (DTPA) violations related to the ban on transgender treatments for minors (SB 14), with the Attorney General arguing for the necessity of the investigation and PFLAG arguing against it based on privacy concerns and lack of relevance.
plaintiff_argument: The Attorney General's office argued that PFLAG's executive director's affidavit provided a reasonable basis to believe PFLAG possessed information relevant to an investigation into medical providers deceptively billing for treatments outlawed by SB 14, and that privacy concerns were addressed by agreed redactions and statutory protections.
defendant_argument: PFLAG, Inc. argued that the requested documents were not relevant to a DTPA investigation, that the Attorney General lacked a valid basis for the demand, and that the CID infringed upon its members' privacy and First and Fourth Amendment rights.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Texas reversed the district court's "Final Declaratory Judgment and Injunction," ruling that PFLAG, Inc. must produce responsive documents to the Attorney General's revised Civil Investigative Demand, subject to recognized privileges and redactions for anonymity.

title: Paxton v. American Oversight
description: Whether district courts have the authority to issue writs of mandamus against constitutional executive officers under the Public Information Act (PIA), with the plaintiff arguing that the PIA grants such authority to district courts, and the defendant arguing that exclusive jurisdiction for such writs against executive officers rests with the Supreme Court.
plaintiff_argument: American Oversight argued that section 552.321(b) of the PIA empowers district courts to issue writs of mandamus against constitutional executive officers, as it is a more specific and later-in-time statute than section 22.002(c).
defendant_argument: The State (Paxton and Abbott) contended that section 552.321(b) is merely a venue provision, not a jurisdictional grant, and that section 22.002(c) of the Government Code reserves exclusive mandamus jurisdiction over constitutional executive officers to the Supreme Court.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the court of appeals and directed the district court to dismiss the mandamus petition for lack of jurisdiction.

title: Texas Department of Family & Protective Services v. Grassroots LeaderShip, Inc.
description: Whether Texas courts are constitutionally authorized to adjudicate moot cases that raise questions of considerable public importance.
plaintiff_argument: Grassroots Leadership, Inc. argued that the case was not moot due to the possibility of re-detention, or if moot, the 'capable-of-repetition yet evading review' exception or the 'public-interest exception' should apply to allow adjudication due to public importance.
defendant_argument: The Texas Department of Family and Protective Services argued that the case was moot, there is no public-interest exception to mootness in Texas, and the court of appeals exceeded its authority by adjudicating a moot case.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the court of appeals' judgment, vacated its decision on the merits, and dismissed the case for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, holding that the 'public-interest exception' violates the Texas Constitution's justiciability limitations.

title: Ex Parte David Leonard Wood
description: Whether the Texas Constitution's due course of law and cruel and unusual punishment clauses prohibit the execution of individuals who are likely not guilty, and what standard of proof should apply to actual innocence claims in capital habeas corpus cases.
plaintiff_argument: The applicant argues that the Texas Constitution prohibits executing those who are likely not guilty, requiring a lower standard of proof (more likely than not) for actual innocence claims in capital cases, and that he should be granted access to DNA testing and a hearing on the merits of his new evidence.
defendant_argument: The state, through the court's previous rulings and statutory writ bar, maintains that the existing 'clear and convincing' standard for actual innocence claims is appropriate, and the majority's remand order, while allowing further evidence development, does not include specific guidance or a directive for DNA testing.
decision_outcome: The Court issued a remand to the lower court for further development of the evidence the Applicant presents, but without specific guidance or a directive for DNA testing.

title: Southern Methodist University v. South Central Jurisdictional Conference of the United Methodist Church
description: Whether Southern Methodist University (SMU) could unilaterally amend its articles of incorporation to remove the South Central Jurisdictional Conference's authority without the Conference's consent, or if Texas law and the church-autonomy doctrine protect the Conference's control.
plaintiff_argument: The Conference argued that SMU's articles of incorporation explicitly require Conference approval for amendments and that Texas law (§ 22.207) and the church-autonomy doctrine protect its right to control SMU.
defendant_argument: SMU argued it could amend its articles without the Conference's consent, that a general limitation on lawsuits (§ 20.002) prevented the Conference's challenge, and that the issue was a private matter not implicating church autonomy.
decision_outcome: The Court held that Texas law (§ 22.207) allows the South Central Jurisdictional Conference to seek judicial interpretation of SMU's articles of incorporation and proceed with its contract claim, thereby vindicating the Conference's rights.

title: Paxton v. Annunciation House
description: Whether the Texas Attorney General has the authority to investigate Annunciation House for allegedly harboring illegal aliens and to seek revocation of its corporate charter, and whether the state's records-request statutes are constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The Attorney General asserts constitutional and statutory authority to investigate Annunciation House for violating Texas law by harboring illegal aliens, to demand access to its records, and to file a quo warranto action to revoke its charter.
defendant_argument: Annunciation House argues that the Attorney General's actions violate its constitutional rights, that the alien-harboring allegations do not constitute illegal harboring under Texas law, are preempted by federal law, unconstitutionally vague, and violate the Texas Religious Freedom Restoration Act.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the trial court's judgment, vacating the injunction against the Attorney General's records requests and allowing the Attorney General to file a quo warranto action against Annunciation House.

title: Stary v. Ethridge
description: Whether constitutional due process requires clear and convincing evidence to support a protective order prohibiting contact between a parent and her children for longer than two years, with the plaintiff arguing it does due to the order's similarity to parental rights termination, and the defendant arguing it does not as such orders are not equivalent to termination and existing safeguards are sufficient.
plaintiff_argument: Christine Stary argued that a lifetime protective order prohibiting contact with her children is tantamount to termination of parental rights, requiring a heightened evidentiary burden of clear and convincing evidence under due process.
defendant_argument: Brady Ethridge (via amicus counsel) argued that lengthy protective orders are not equivalent to parental rights termination, as they leave some ancillary rights intact and allow for review, thus not requiring a heightened burden of proof.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the court of appeals' judgment and remanded the case to the trial court for a new hearing, holding that constitutional due process requires clear and convincing evidence to support a protective order prohibiting all contact between a parent and her children for a period exceeding two years, and that the child's best interest must be considered.

title: Commons of Lake Houston v. City of Houston
description: Whether a regulatory taking can occur even when the regulation at issue is intended to promote public health, safety, and general welfare, is a valid exercise of the government's police power, and is designed to ensure compliance with the federal National Flood Insurance Program.
plaintiff_argument: The Commons argues that the City's amended floodplain ordinance, despite being a valid exercise of police power and for federal program compliance, caused a regulatory taking of its property under the Texas Constitution, rendering many lots undevelopable and destroying expected profits, and that such a claim is viable, ripe, and they have standing.
defendant_argument: The City argues that The Commons failed to allege a valid takings claim because the amended ordinance was a valid exercise of its police power and designed to comply with the National Flood Insurance Program, and therefore cannot constitute a compensable taking. The City also contended the claim was unripe and The Commons lacked standing.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Texas reversed the court of appeals' judgment, holding that a regulatory-takings claim can be asserted even if the regulation is a valid exercise of police power or for federal program compliance, and that The Commons's claim is ripe and they have standing, remanding the case for further proceedings.

title: Perez v. City of San Antonio
description: Whether Article I, Section 6-a of the Texas Constitution imposes a categorical bar on any limitation of any religious service, regardless of the sort of limitation and the government's interest in that limitation.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Section 6-a imposes a categorical bar on any limitation of religious services, not even allowing the City to satisfy strict scrutiny.
defendant_argument: The City of San Antonio (implicitly, and as supported by the majority) argued that Section 6-a does not impose a categorical bar, and limitations are permissible, especially for government interests like preserving public lands.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that Article I, Section 6-a of the Texas Constitution does not impose a categorical bar on limitations of religious services that result from the government's preservation and maintenance of public lands.

title: Elliott v. City of College Station
description: Whether local regulation of property owners in an extraterritorial jurisdiction (ETJ) without corresponding voting rights is incompatible with the Texas Constitution's "republican form of government".
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that local regulation of their property in the City's ETJ without the right to vote in City elections is unconstitutional under the Texas Constitution's "republican form of government" and seek to void the ordinances.
defendant_argument: The City argues the constitutional claim is nonjusticiable, asserting that the form of local government is a political question for the legislature, not the courts, and that plaintiffs lack standing and the claims are not ripe.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the lower court judgments and remanded the case, instructing the trial court to abate proceedings to allow the property owners a reasonable opportunity to complete the statutory opt-out process.

title: Ex parte Charette
description: Whether the Texas Ethics Commission (TEC) has exclusive jurisdiction over alleged campaign-law violations, requiring exhaustion of administrative remedies before criminal prosecution can proceed, or if prosecutors can initiate criminal charges independently.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecution was unauthorized because the Texas Ethics Commission (TEC) has exclusive jurisdiction over campaign-law violations, and its administrative process, including a referral for criminal prosecution, was a prerequisite that was not followed, thus violating her due process rights.
defendant_argument: District and county attorneys have constitutional authority to prosecute crimes, and the TEC's civil enforcement scheme does not grant it exclusive jurisdiction over criminal matters, nor does it prevent prosecutors from initiating criminal charges independently.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the court of appeals' judgment and ordered the dismissal of the indictments, holding that the trial court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because the TEC has exclusive jurisdiction over the initial determination of campaign law violations.

title: In re Dallas County
description: Whether S.B. 1045, which creates the Fifteenth Court of Appeals with statewide jurisdiction and specific judicial appointment/election procedures, is constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: Dallas County argues that S.B. 1045 is unconstitutional because the Fifteenth Court's statewide geographic reach and subject-matter jurisdictional scope violate the Texas Constitution, and its justices are unconstitutionally installed due to delayed elections.
defendant_argument: The state officials (HHSC) implicitly argue that S.B. 1045 is constitutional, asserting that the legislature has the authority to create the Fifteenth Court with statewide jurisdiction and to define its jurisdictional scope and the process for appointing and electing its justices.
decision_outcome: The court denied Dallas County's request for relief, holding that S.B. 1045 is constitutional, including the creation of the Fifteenth Court of Appeals, its jurisdictional provisions, and the appointment process for its justices.

title: Borgelt v. Austin Firefighters Association
description: Whether Article 10 of the collective-bargaining agreement, which grants "Association Business Leave" to firefighters, violates the Texas Constitution's "Gift Clauses" by making an unconstitutional gift of public resources to a private party.
plaintiff_argument: Petitioners argue that Article 10, as written and/or implemented, violates the Gift Clauses because it impermissibly benefits the Austin Firefighters Association by providing paid leave for improper, private, or political purposes, without sufficient public control or return consideration.
defendant_argument: Respondents argue that Article 10 does not violate the Gift Clauses because it serves a legitimate public purpose, provides sufficient return consideration, and the City retains control over the funds, and that alleged improper uses are not authorized by the agreement itself.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that Article 10 of the collective-bargaining agreement does not facially violate the Gift Clauses, but reversed the award of fees and sanctions against the petitioners.

title: In re State
description: Whether Harris County's Uplift Harris program, which provides no-strings-attached cash payments to individuals, violates the Texas Constitution's prohibition on gratuitous payments or if it qualifies as a permissible economic development program.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that the Uplift Harris program is unconstitutional as it constitutes "gratuitous payments to individuals" and lacks public control over the disbursed funds, violating the Texas Constitution.
defendant_argument: Harris County argues that the Uplift Harris program is a permissible exercise of its freedom to implement the program and qualifies as "economic development" under the Texas Constitution, section 52-a, as it aims to boost the economy.
decision_outcome: The court granted the State's motion for temporary relief, ordering Harris County to refrain from distributing funds under the Uplift Harris program until further order of the Court, pending the underlying appeal.

title: Texas Department of Transportation v. Self
description: Whether the Texas Department of Transportation (TxDOT) is liable for the destruction of trees on private property, either due to negligence under the Tort Claims Act or as an intentional taking under inverse condemnation.
plaintiff_argument: The Selfs argued that TxDOT waived immunity for negligence because the subcontractor's employees were TxDOT employees or TxDOT employees operated the equipment, and that TxDOT intentionally directed the destruction of their trees, constituting inverse condemnation.
defendant_argument: TxDOT argued that immunity for negligence was not waived as the subcontractor's employees were not TxDOT employees and no TxDOT employees operated the equipment, and that it lacked the requisite intent for inverse condemnation, believing the trees were within its right-of-way.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed the Selfs' negligence cause of action against TxDOT but reversed the court of appeals' judgment on the inverse condemnation claim, remanding it to the trial court for further proceedings.

title: Hogan v. Southern Methodist University
description: Whether the application of the Pandemic Liability Protection Act to Hogan's breach-of-contract claim violates the retroactivity clause in article I, section 16 of the Texas Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Hogan argued that the Pandemic Liability Protection Act (PLPA) retroactively withdrew his pre-existing right to hold Southern Methodist University (SMU) liable for breach of contract for not providing in-person education, thereby violating the Texas Constitution's prohibition on "retroactive law[s]".
defendant_argument: Southern Methodist University (SMU), protected by the PLPA, argued that the Act shields educational institutions from monetary liability for changes made due to pandemic emergencies and government orders, and that Hogan had no settled expectation of recovery for in-person education that became impossible.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the application of the Pandemic Liability Protection Act to Hogan's breach-of-contract claim does not violate the retroactivity clause in article I, section 16 of the Texas Constitution.

title: Texas v. Loe
description: Whether the Legislature's prohibition of certain medical treatments for children suffering from gender dysphoria violates the Texas Constitution, with plaintiffs arguing it infringes on parental rights, physicians' occupational freedom, and discriminates against transgender adolescents, while defendants argue it is a constitutional and rational policy choice to regulate medicine and protect children.
plaintiff_argument: The statute is unconstitutional because it infringes on parents' fundamental right to make medical decisions for their children, deprives Texas physicians of their occupational freedom, and discriminates against transgender adolescents based on sex, sex stereotypes, and transgender status.
defendant_argument: The statute is a permissible and rational policy choice by the Legislature to regulate the practice of medicine and protect the health and wellbeing of children, and it does not unconstitutionally infringe on parental rights, physicians' occupational freedom, or discriminate.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Texas reversed and vacated the trial court's temporary injunction order, concluding that the plaintiffs failed to establish a probable right to relief on any of their asserted constitutional violations.

title: City of Dallas v. Employees Retirement Fund of City of Dallas
description: Whether a city ordinance may bestow on a third party the perpetual right to veto categories of future lawmaking.
plaintiff_argument: The City of Dallas argued that its ordinance imposing term limits on the Fund's board was valid because the board's veto power was an unconstitutional delegation of legislative authority and therefore unenforceable.
defendant_argument: The Employees' Retirement Fund argued that its governing chapter was a "trust document" requiring board consent for amendments, and the City's term-limit ordinance was an invalid amendment without such consent.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the court of appeals' judgment, holding that the board's veto power over city law is unenforceable because a legislative body cannot bind its successors or alienate its lawmaking authority.

title: Becerra v. State
description: Whether an alternate juror's presence and participation, including voting, during jury deliberations violates constitutional and statutory provisions regarding jury composition and outside influence, and what harm analysis standard applies to such violations.
plaintiff_argument: The alternate juror's participation in deliberations and a preliminary vote on guilt violated his constitutional right to a twelve-person jury and statutory prohibitions against unauthorized persons being with or conversing with the jury, requiring a new trial or remand with a presumption of harm.
defendant_argument: The alternate juror's presence did not violate constitutional or statutory jury size requirements because the ultimate verdict was rendered by twelve regular jurors, and any statutory violation was harmless or the presumption of harm was rebutted.
decision_outcome: The Court held that the alternate juror's presence and participation in deliberations violated statutory prohibitions against unauthorized persons, but did not violate constitutional or statutory twelve-person jury requirements. The case was remanded for the court of appeals to conduct a harm analysis under Rule 44.2(b), disavowing the rebuttable presumption of harm for Article 36.22 violations.

title: Hensley v. State Commission on Judicial Conduct
description: Whether a judge was required to exhaust administrative remedies before suing the State Commission on Judicial Conduct for alleged violations of the Texas Religious Freedom Restoration Act.
plaintiff_argument: The judge argued she was not required to exhaust administrative remedies because the administrative process could not provide the full relief she sought and her suit was not a collateral attack on the warning.
defendant_argument: The State Commission on Judicial Conduct (as supported by the dissenting opinion) argued the judge was required to exhaust administrative remedies because the statutory scheme provides exclusive jurisdiction and an effective method for review, and exhaustion could have mooted her claims.
decision_outcome: The Court held that the judge was not required to exhaust her administrative remedies, thereby allowing her lawsuit against the State Commission on Judicial Conduct to proceed.

title: Zurawski v. Texas
description: Whether Texas's Human Life Protection Act, which permits life-saving abortions, is unconstitutionally narrow in its definition of "life-threatening physical condition" and "reasonable medical judgment," or if the current law is sufficiently broad and constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Human Life Protection Act is unclear, too narrow, and unconstitutional, leading doctors to delay or refuse abortions even when permitted by law, and sought a broader interpretation or rewriting of the law to include more circumstances such as unsafe pregnancies or untreatable fetal conditions.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the Human Life Protection Act is clear, constitutional, and already permits abortions when a life-threatening physical condition places the mother at risk of death or serious physical impairment, and that the trial court's injunction improperly expanded the law.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the trial court's temporary injunction, upholding the existing Texas Human Life Protection Act's interpretation.

title: Harris County v. Texas
description: Whether Senate Bill 1750, which reorganizes election administration in Harris County, is an unconstitutional local law, with Harris County arguing it is unconstitutional and would cause irreparable harm to election administration, while the State Officer Defendants implicitly argue for its enforcement.
plaintiff_argument: Harris County argues that Senate Bill 1750 is an unconstitutional local law that would cause imminent and irreparable injury by disrupting election administration, leading to inefficiencies, disorganization, confusion, and increased costs, and jeopardizing the validity of the November Election.
defendant_argument: The State Officer Defendants (Interim Attorney General and Secretary of State) implicitly argue for the enforcement of Senate Bill 1750, which would abolish the Harris County Elections Administrator position and transfer its responsibilities, suggesting it is a valid law.
decision_outcome: The court granted Harris County's request for a temporary injunction, preventing the State Officer Defendants from enforcing Senate Bill 1750 until all issues in the lawsuit are finally determined.

title: Ex parte Sheffield
description: Whether speedy trial claims are cognizable in pretrial habeas corpus when an applicant seeks a speedy trial rather than dismissal, especially when trial is indefinitely postponed due to administrative orders.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that speedy trial claims are cognizable in pretrial habeas corpus under the Ex parte Perry rule, particularly when seeking a speedy trial and when trial is indefinitely postponed due to administrative fiat, as the right would otherwise be undermined.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that speedy trial claims are not cognizable in pretrial habeas corpus because allowing such claims would improperly lead to interlocutory appeals, inject appellate delay, and ultimately undermine the speedy trial right, and that the Perry rule does not apply.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the judgment of the court of appeals, holding that speedy trial claims are not cognizable in pretrial habeas corpus and that the Ex parte Perry rule does not provide an exception for indefinitely postponed trials; the proper remedy is a motion to dismiss followed by appeal, or a writ of mandamus if trial is indefinitely postponed.

title: Hotze v. Turner
description: Whether the City of Houston's 'primacy clause,' which required a citizen-initiated charter amendment to receive more votes than a council-initiated amendment to become effective, conflicts with state law requiring adoption by a simple majority vote, and whether the City can indefinitely delay the effectiveness of an adopted charter amendment.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the primacy clause violates state law requiring cities to adopt proposed charter amendments when voters approve them by a majority vote, and that the City cannot indefinitely delay the effectiveness of an adopted amendment.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the primacy clause does not conflict with state law as the statute only requires adoption, not immediate effectiveness, and that the City has discretion to delay an amendment's effectiveness or that the two amendments irreconcilably conflict.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Texas reversed the court of appeals' judgment in part, ruling that the City of Houston's 'primacy clause' is void for conflicting with state law, and remanded the case to the trial court to determine how to harmonize the two voter-approved charter amendments, while affirming the City's compliance with Proposition 1.

title: City of Houston v. Houston Proffesional Fire Fighters Association
description: Whether Chapter 174 of the Local Government Code, which governs firefighter collective bargaining and compensation standards, is constitutional and preempts a local pay-parity amendment.
plaintiff_argument: The Fire Fighters argued that Chapter 174 is constitutional, waives governmental immunity for the City, and its state-level compensation standards preempt the local pay-parity amendment.
defendant_argument: The City of Houston and Houston Police Officers' Union argued that Chapter 174's judicial enforcement provisions are unconstitutional, the City retains governmental immunity, and Chapter 174 does not preempt the local pay-parity amendment.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed that Chapter 174 is constitutional and waives the City's immunity, but reversed the lower court's decision on preemption, ruling that Chapter 174 does preempt the local pay-parity amendment.

title: The Lilith Fund for Reproductive Equity v. Dickson
description: Whether statements equating abortion to murder and characterizing abortion providers as "criminal" are defamatory false statements of fact or constitutionally protected opinions in the context of public debate.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the defendant's statements falsely characterized abortion as murder and labeled them "criminal organizations," which is legally defamatory because abortion was not murder under Texas law at the time.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued his statements were protected opinions about abortion law and its interpretation, made in pursuit of changing the law, and thus not defamatory.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Texas affirmed the dismissal of the defamation suit, holding that the challenged statements were protected opinion about abortion law and free speech, not verifiable false statements of fact.

title: Virlar v. Puente
description: Whether Chapter 33 of the Civil Practice and Remedies Code requires a credit for a family member's settlement against the judgment, and whether Chapter 74 of the Texas Medical Liability Act requires periodic payments of damages for future medical expenses.
plaintiff_argument: Puente argued that her daughter's settlement should not be credited against her damages and that periodic payments for future medical expenses were not required.
defendant_argument: Virlar and Gonzaba argued that Chapter 33 required a credit for the daughter's settlement and that the TMLA required periodic payments for future medical expenses.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the court of appeals' judgment in part, holding that the trial court improperly denied a credit for C.P.'s settlement and an award of periodic payments for future medical expenses, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: State v. Aktiengesellschaft
description: Whether the Governor's appointment of substitute justices to the Supreme Court of Texas, in a case where the State is a party, violates due process or creates an appearance of impropriety, thereby requiring the Chief Justice to withdraw the certification letter and dismiss the petitions.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Texas implicitly argued that the Governor's appointment of substitute justices is a valid statutory process that does not violate due process or create an appearance of partiality, and therefore, the Respondents' requests should be denied.
defendant_argument: The Respondents argued that allowing the Governor to appoint justices in this case would create due-process and ethical problems, effectively allowing the State to "be the judge of its own cause," and that the Chief Justice should rescind the request and dismiss the petitions.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Texas denied the Respondents' requests to withdraw the Chief Justice's certification letter and to dismiss the petitions as improvidently granted, ruling that the Governor's appointment of substitute justices does not create a serious risk of actual bias or violate due-process provisions.

title: Nath v. Texas Children's Hospital
description: Whether Dr. Rahul Nath was entitled to a jury trial to determine the reasonableness and necessity of attorney's fees awarded as sanctions, with Nath arguing for the right to a jury trial on this issue and the Hospital and Baylor arguing that the law-of-the-case doctrine bars this request.
plaintiff_argument: Dr. Rahul Nath contends he is entitled to a jury finding on the amount of attorney's fees the Hospital and Baylor reasonably and necessarily incurred, citing the constitutional right to a jury trial.
defendant_argument: Texas Children's Hospital and Baylor College of Medicine argue that the law-of-the-case doctrine bars Nath from renewing his request for a jury trial on attorney's fees, and that Nath waived the complaint.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Texas denied Dr. Nath's petition for review, thereby affirming the lower court's decision to uphold the $1.4 million attorney-fee-shifting sanction without a jury trial on the fee amount.

title: Texas Department of State Health Services v. Crown Distributing LLC
description: Whether the Texas law prohibiting the manufacturing and processing of smokable hemp products violates the state's due-course clause by infringing on economic liberty and worker rights.
plaintiff_argument: The state's ban on manufacturing and processing smokable hemp products violates the Texas Constitution's due-course clause because it infringes on their right to a lawful occupation and is an oppressive economic regulation.
defendant_argument: The due-course clause does not protect the Hemp Companies' interest in manufacturing or processing smokable hemp products because it is not a "lawful calling" and was previously illegal.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the trial court's judgment, holding that the due-course clause does not protect the Hemp Companies' asserted interest in manufacturing and processing smokable hemp products, but the injunction against distribution and retail sale remains.

title: Abbott v. Mexican American Legislative Caucus
description: Whether Texas's reapportionment laws (H.B. 1 and S.B. 4) violate Article III, Sections 26 and 28 of the Texas Constitution, with plaintiffs arguing they do and defendants arguing they do not.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that H.B. 1 violates the county-line rule (Article III, Section 26) by not providing enough wholly contained districts for Cameron County, and that H.B. 1 and S.B. 4 violate Article III, Section 28 by being enacted during a special session rather than the first regular session after the census.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the plaintiffs lacked standing, their claims were moot, and were barred by sovereign immunity, asserting that the reapportionment laws complied with constitutional requirements or that Section 28 did not prohibit apportionment at other times.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed the Mexican American Legislative Caucus's claims and the Gutierrez Plaintiffs' Section 28 claim for lack of jurisdiction, but remanded the Gutierrez Plaintiffs' Section 26 claim to the trial court for repleading against a proper defendant.

title: Fire Protection Service v. Survitec Survival Products
description: Whether the application of the Fair Practices of Equipment Manufacturers, Distributors, Wholesalers, and Dealers Act to a preexisting at-will agreement violates the Texas Constitution's prohibition against retroactive laws.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, FPS, argued that the Act should apply to the agreement and that Survitec's constitutional challenge was improperly brought under the retroactivity clause instead of the contracts clause, and that Survitec violated the Act by terminating their agreement without good cause.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Survitec, argued that applying the Act to their preexisting at-will agreement unconstitutionally retroactively eliminated their right to terminate the relationship at will, and that the grace period provided was insufficient notice to adapt to the new law.
decision_outcome: The court concluded that the application of the Act to Survitec's termination of the agreement does not violate the constitutional prohibition against retroactive laws.

title: City of Baytown v. Schrock
description: Whether the City of Baytown's utility enforcement actions, including refusing service and placing a lien, constituted a constitutional taking of Alan Schrock's property requiring compensation.
plaintiff_argument: The City's improper actions, such as withholding utility service and placing a lien, resulted in a loss of rental income and property value, constituting a taking under the Texas or United States Constitution.
defendant_argument: The City's enforcement actions were not an intentional taking for public use, but rather a means to collect outstanding utility bills, and Schrock failed to establish a constitutional right to compensation.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the court of appeals' judgment and reinstated the trial court's directed verdict, ruling that the City's utility enforcement actions did not establish a regulatory taking of private property as a matter of law.

title: State v. Stephens
description: Whether Section 273.021 of the Texas Election Code, which authorizes the Attorney General (AG) to prosecute election law offenses, violates the Texas Constitution's Separation of Powers Clause, with the plaintiff arguing it does and the defendant arguing it does not.
plaintiff_argument: The Attorney General lacked constitutional authority to independently prosecute election law offenses, violating the separation of powers, and therefore the indictment against her should be dismissed.
defendant_argument: The Attorney General has the authority to prosecute election law offenses, and the Court's original opinion finding a constitutional violation and ordering dismissal of the indictment was flawed and should be reconsidered.
decision_outcome: The Court denied the Attorney General's motion for rehearing, thereby upholding its original decision that Section 273.021 of the Texas Election Code, which authorizes the AG to prosecute election law offenses, violates the Texas Constitution's Separation of Powers Clause, and maintaining the dismissal of Stephens's indictment.

title: In re Abbott
description: Whether the Texas Constitution grants the House of Representatives the authority to physically compel the attendance of absent members to achieve a quorum.
plaintiff_argument: The House's power to "compel attendance" only allows for persuasion and dialogue, not physical restraint or arrest, and the district court's temporary restraining order was valid.
defendant_argument: The Texas Constitution explicitly grants the House the authority to physically compel the attendance of absent members, including by arrest, to ensure a quorum, and the district court abused its discretion by issuing the TRO.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court ruled that the Texas Constitution empowers the House of Representatives to physically compel the attendance of absent members and directed the district court to withdraw its temporary restraining order.

title: Odyssey 2020 Academy, Inc. v. Galveston Central Appraisal District
description: Whether property leased by a public open-enrollment charter school with state funds is exempt from ad valorem taxes, with the plaintiff arguing for exemption as public property and the defendant arguing against it because the property is not actually publicly owned.
plaintiff_argument: Odyssey contends it is entitled to an exemption from ad valorem taxes for privately owned property it leases for a public charter school, arguing that state law considers such property public for all purposes, including tax exemption.
defendant_argument: The District argues that Odyssey is not entitled to an exemption because it only has a leasehold interest, not legal or equitable title, and the Constitution does not allow recharacterizing privately owned property as publicly owned for tax exemption.
decision_outcome: The court overruled Odyssey's issues and affirmed the court of appeals' judgment, denying the requested tax exemption.

title: Texas State University v. Villarreal
description: Whether a state university's dismissal of a student for poor academic performance implicates a liberty or property interest protected by the Texas Constitution's guarantee of due course of law.
plaintiff_argument: Villarreal argued that his academic dismissal, stemming from the university's mishandling of a cheating investigation, deprived him of his liberty and property interests in his graduate education without due course of law, violating the Texas Constitution.
defendant_argument: Texas Southern University argued that academic dismissal for poor performance does not implicate a protected liberty or property interest under the Texas Constitution, and even if it did, the procedures followed were constitutionally adequate.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the court of appeals' judgment, holding that academic dismissal for poor performance does not implicate a protected liberty interest and that the university provided adequate procedural due course of law, thereby dismissing Villarreal's constitutional claims.

title: Texas Propane Gas Association v. City of Houston
description: Whether civil courts have subject-matter jurisdiction to adjudicate a preemption claim against local regulations that carry criminal penalties, and whether the Texas Propane Gas Association (TPGA) has standing to challenge all of the City of Houston's liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) regulations en masse.
plaintiff_argument: The Texas Propane Gas Association (TPGA) argued that the City of Houston's local LPG regulations are preempted by state law and that civil courts have jurisdiction to hear its preemption claim, even if the local regulations include criminal penalties, as the essence of the case is civil and threatens irreparable injury to property rights. TPGA also argued it has standing to challenge all the City's LPG regulations due to the burden of inconsistent local rules.
defendant_argument: The City of Houston argued that civil courts lack subject-matter jurisdiction because its local LPG regulations carry criminal penalties, making it a 'criminal law matter' that should be raised in defense to prosecution. The City also contended that TPGA lacks standing to challenge all its LPG regulations without demonstrating specific injury for each discrete regulation challenged.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the judgment of the court of appeals, ruling that civil courts have subject-matter jurisdiction over TPGA's preemption claim and that TPGA has standing to challenge the City's LPG regulations, and remanded the case to the trial court for further proceedings.

title: Dulin v. State
description: Whether the time payment fee was prematurely assessed.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the time payment fee was unconstitutional, violating the principle of separation of powers.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the time payment fee was prematurely assessed because it was levied before the statutory 31-day period elapsed.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the time payment fee was prematurely assessed because an appeal suspends the obligation to pay court costs, vacating the lower court's judgment and remanding the case.
